title: Deadlock, Livelock & Starvation
scopeHtml: Coffman conditions and prevention, reading thread dumps, livelock/starvation/priority inversion, pool-starvation deadlock, contention diagnosis, and production cascades (blocked request threads, connection pool exhaustion).

questions.promptHtml: What are the four conditions required for a deadlock, and how does each one map to a prevention technique in Java code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you reason about deadlock structurally (break one condition) rather than reciting "use lock ordering".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Remove any one and deadlock is impossible. In practice I break circular wait with a global lock order, hold-and-wait by acquiring everything up front or using one coarser lock, and no-preemption with tryLock(timeout) and back-off. Mutual exclusion is usually what I want to keep, so I reduce it with immutability or lock-free structures where possible.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Condition Meaning Java prevention
Mutual exclusion Resource held by one thread at a time Immutable data, ConcurrentHashMap, atomics, message passing (shrinks the set of locks)
Hold and wait Thread holds lock A while requesting B Acquire all locks atomically (single coarser lock), or release A before taking B
No preemption Lock cannot be forcibly taken ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout): on failure release everything and retry
Circular wait T1 waits on T2 waits on ... T1 Total order on locks (by id, by System.identityHashCode + tie-breaker lock)

synchronized gives you no way to back out (no timeout, no interrupt while blocked on monitor entry), so with intrinsic locks the only practical levers are ordering and coarsening. ReentrantLock gives you tryLock, lockInterruptibly, and thus preemption-like recovery.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Break "no preemption": back off and retry instead of blocking forever
boolean lockBoth(ReentrantLock a, ReentrantLock b) throws InterruptedException {
    if (a.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        try {
            if (b.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return true; // caller unlocks both
        } catch (Throwable t) { a.unlock(); throw t; }
        a.unlock();
    }
    return false; // caller sleeps a randomized delay, then retries
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "synchronized causes deadlock". Locks are fine; the cycle is the problem.
  • Retrying tryLock in lock-step without randomized back-off turns deadlock into livelock (see Q183).
  • Believing a single lock cannot deadlock: it can if the holder waits on something that needs the lock (e.g. waiting for a task on the same pool, Q185).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which condition is cheapest to break in a bank-transfer method? → Circular wait via ordered locking by account id.
  2. Can a single-lock program deadlock? → Yes, via resources other than locks: thread pools, connection pools, latches, join().
  3. Can the JVM detect all four-condition cycles? → Only monitor and AbstractOwnableSynchronizer cycles; not pool/latch/DB cycles (Q190).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the four conditions and says "lock ordering". Senior maps each to a concrete tactic, knows synchronized cannot be preempted, and widens "resource" to pools, latches and DB rows.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Most real deadlocks in services are not two synchronized blocks but a thread waiting on a resource (pool slot, future) held by a thread waiting on the first.

questions.promptHtml: Show a minimal two-lock deadlock in Java and fix it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline: can you write and fix the canonical bug, including the dynamic-order case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Thread 1 locks A then B, thread 2 locks B then A; each ends up holding one and waiting for the other. The fix is a single global acquisition order. When the locks are chosen dynamically, like transfer(from, to), I order by a stable unique key such as account id.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The static case is fixed by convention (document "always A before B"). The dynamic case is where interviews bite: transfer(a, b) in one thread and transfer(b, a) in another form the same cycle although the code order looks identical. Ordering by id fixes it. System.identityHashCode can collide, so a tie-break lock is needed if you use it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: lock order depends on argument order
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); } }
}

// Fixed: order by unique id
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
    Account second = first == from ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting from == to (reentrant for synchronized, so fine, but ordering code must not break on it).
  • Ordering by hashCode() that users can override and collide.
  • Calling alien code (callbacks, overridable methods) while holding a lock: it can take locks you do not know about.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if ids can be equal? → Use a global tie-breaker lock around the rare tie.
  2. Why is calling a listener under lock dangerous? → Open call: unknown lock order. Copy state, release, then call.
  3. Can static analysis help? → Yes: IntelliJ/ErrorProne @GuardedBy checks, and lock-order tools (e.g. JCStress is not it; use code review plus runtime tests with ThreadMXBean).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE fixes the static example. Senior handles the dynamic order, tie-breaking, and open calls under lock.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "transfer between two entities" path with an in-memory lock per entity deadlocks only when two opposite transfers race: rare in tests, certain at scale.

questions.promptHtml: A service hangs. Walk me through confirming a Java-level deadlock from a thread dump and what you look at in the output.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tooling fluency under incident conditions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I take 3 dumps 5-10 seconds apart with jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l (or jstack -l). If there is a monitor or j.u.c lock cycle, HotSpot prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end listing each thread, the lock it waits for, and who holds it. I confirm the same threads are stuck in all dumps. If there is no such banner but threads are parked, it is a non-lock deadlock (pool, latch, DB) and I trace what they wait on.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l includes "Locked ownable synchronizers", needed to see ReentrantLock holders. Plain jstack without -l hides them.
  • Lines to read: - waiting to lock <0x...> (a Foo) (BLOCKED on monitor), - locked <0x...>, and for j.u.c: - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync) with state WAITING (parking) and the owner listed under "Locked ownable synchronizers" of another thread.
  • The deadlock detector covers synchronized and ownable synchronizers (Oracle troubleshooting guide); it does not cover latches, Future.get, pool starvation, or DB locks.
  • Programmatic: ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() (monitors + ownable synchronizers) vs findMonitorDeadlockedThreads() (monitors only).
  • Container: kill -3 <pid> writes the dump to stdout; jcmd needs same user/PID namespace as the JVM (run via kubectl exec).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();      // null if none
if (ids != null) {
    for (ThreadInfo ti : mx.getThreadInfo(ids, true, true)) {
        log.error("DEADLOCK {} waits on {} owned by {}",
            ti.getThreadName(), ti.getLockName(), ti.getLockOwnerName());
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A single dump: a thread BLOCKED once may just be contended. Same stack across dumps means stuck.
  • Using jstack without -l and missing ReentrantLock owners.
  • Assuming no banner means no deadlock.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Thread is WAITING (parking) with no owner shown? → Probably a latch, Future.get, or condition; look for who should signal it.
  2. App is too hung to attach? → kill -3, or a -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError-style pre-arranged watchdog; JFR continuous recording also has thread dump events.
  3. Can you run detection inside the app? → Yes, schedule findDeadlockedThreads() every N seconds and alert/export a metric.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE runs jstack and reads the banner. Senior takes repeated dumps with -l, knows what the detector misses, and wires an in-process detector.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams lose hours because the dump lacked -l, so the ReentrantLock owner was invisible.

questions.promptHtml: What is livelock, how does it differ from deadlock, and how did a tryLock-based fix produce one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know that the standard deadlock fix has its own failure mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In deadlock threads are blocked and make no progress; in livelock they are running, burning CPU, reacting to each other, and still make no progress. A classic cause is two threads using tryLock on two locks, both failing, both releasing and retrying in sync. Fix with randomized exponential back-off, or an ordering that makes one side always win.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Symptoms differ: deadlock = threads in BLOCKED/WAITING, CPU idle. Livelock = threads RUNNABLE or cycling through short sleeps, CPU elevated, throughput zero; thread dumps differ each time but show the same retry loop. Variants: retry storms between services (A retries B, B retries A), optimistic CAS loops under extreme contention, and message ping-pong. Remedy: jitter, bounded retries, backing off by thread-specific amounts, or a coordinator that assigns priority.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Livelock-prone: both threads loop in lock step
while (!(a.tryLock() && b.tryLock())) { release(a, b); /* retry immediately */ }

// Better: bounded, randomized back-off
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (a.tryLock()) {
        if (b.tryLock()) return true;
        a.unlock();
    }
    Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1L << i, 2L << i)); // ms
}
return false; // surface failure rather than spin forever

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying with a fixed sleep: both sides stay synchronized.
  • Unbounded retries hide the problem as "slowness".
  • Not releasing the first lock on failure (that makes it a real deadlock).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you recognise it in prod? → High CPU, zero progress, repeating stack in several dumps, retry counters climbing.
  2. Is a CAS retry loop livelock? → Lock-free means some thread progresses; LongAdder reduces contention for hot counters.
  3. Service-level livelock? → Mutual retries without jitter or retry budgets; add jitter and a retry budget.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines it. Senior ties it to retry storms and tryLock loops and names jitter and bounded retries.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Two services with synchronized retry timers kept re-driving each other after an outage; jitter ended the storm.

questions.promptHtml: What is thread starvation, and how can it occur even though no deadlock exists? Does ReentrantLock(true) solve it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks the difference between "no progress for anyone" and "no progress for someone", and fairness cost awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Starvation is a thread being perpetually denied a resource while others progress. Causes: unfair locks and barging, a writer starved by constant readers, high-priority tasks monopolizing a pool, or a long task hogging a single-thread queue. A fair lock gives FIFO-ish acquisition and prevents lock starvation but typically cuts throughput significantly, so I use it only when starvation is a proven problem.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Default ReentrantLock and synchronized are non-fair: a running thread can barge ahead of parked waiters, which gives better throughput (no context switch for the barger) but can starve waiters.
  • ReentrantReadWriteLock non-fair mode: waiting writer typically blocks new readers only if it is at the head of the queue, but heavy read traffic can still delay writers; fair mode orders by arrival.
  • Pools: a PriorityBlockingQueue keeps serving high priority; low priority never runs. A shared pool where one tenant's bulk jobs fill the queue starves everyone else's short tasks.
  • Fairness note: even fair ReentrantLock does not guarantee scheduler fairness, and tryLock() without args ignores fairness (barges).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ReentrantLock fair = new ReentrantLock(true); // FIFO among waiting threads
// Isolation instead of fairness for pools:
ExecutorService interactive = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
ExecutorService bulk = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); // bulk can never take interactive threads

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Turning on fair locks everywhere "to be safe".
  • Calling it deadlock because latency is infinite for one request.
  • Ignoring queue discipline (unbounded FIFO with a long head-of-line job).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the default lock unfair? → Throughput: avoids parking/unparking handoff.
  2. How to prevent tenant starvation in a pool? → Separate pools/bulkheads or per-tenant quotas.
  3. How to spot it? → One request class with huge queue time but healthy averages; per-class latency histograms.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use a fair lock". Senior says fairness has a cost, fixes structurally with bulkheads and bounded queues, and measures per-class wait time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Batch export jobs sharing a pool with API calls pushed API p99 from 80 ms to seconds with zero errors.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service runs in-memory per-user locks (to keep a 2 ms critical section off the DB). After a release, once or twice a day a few hundred requests hang; the node needs a restart. CPU is 3%, heap fine. Dump shows two threads BLOCKED on UserLock objects. Code:

void transfer(String fromId, String toId, long amt) {
    Object l1 = locks.computeIfAbsent(fromId, k -> new Object());
    Object l2 = locks.computeIfAbsent(toId, k -> new Object());
    Object first = fromId.hashCode() < toId.hashCode() ? l1 : l2;
    Object second = first == l1 ? l2 : l1;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { move(fromId, toId, amt); } }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and fix it. Why does it only show up once or twice a day?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks ordered, so maybe the DB is slow." Or claims ordering by hashCode is a guaranteed fix, without considering collisions and computeIfAbsent races.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are user ids arbitrary strings (collisions plausible)? Does locks grow forever? Can fromId == toId? Is this single node or sharded by user?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart or route traffic away; add a thread-dump on health-check failure so the next occurrence is captured with -l.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) String.hashCode() collision: two different ids with equal hashCode, so < is false for both orderings, and the two transfers pick opposite orders. (b) Same id both ways: harmless (reentrant). (c) locks map memory growth (not the hang). Red herring: DB slowness (CPU idle and dump shows monitors).
  4. How to verify: jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l: banner "Found one Java-level deadlock" with two UserLock monitors. Check the two ids: "Aa".hashCode() == "BB".hashCode() is a well-known collision pair (both 2112). Replay with such ids in a unit test.
  5. Root cause: Order is defined by a non-unique key. When hashCodes tie, fromId.hashCode() < toId.hashCode() is false in both calls, so first is l2 for A->B (=toId's lock) and for B->A is its own l2 = A's lock: opposite order, cycle. Rare because real ids rarely collide, hence once or twice a day.
  6. Fix: Order by a total order: fromId.compareTo(toId) (unique strings), handle equality separately.
int c = fromId.compareTo(toId);
Object a = locks.computeIfAbsent(c <= 0 ? fromId : toId, k -> new Object());
Object b = locks.computeIfAbsent(c <= 0 ? toId : fromId, k -> new Object());
synchronized (a) { if (c == 0) { move(...); } else synchronized (b) { move(fromId, toId, amt); } }

Long term: stripe locks (locks[floorMod(id.hashCode(), 256)]) with ordered stripe indices plus a tie-break when stripes equal; or push serialization into the DB (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ordered by id). 7. Prevention: Unit test with the colliding strings; property test with random ids and concurrent opposite transfers and a findDeadlockedThreads watchdog; code review rule "order by a unique total key". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add tryLock timeouts to paper over it silently; failing transfers randomly is worse than deterministic ordering. I would not use identityHashCode alone, it also can collide.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not synchronized on the interned id string? → Strings are shared globally; unrelated code can lock the same object.
  • The map grows unbounded, what now? → Striping, or Striped<Lock> (Guava); use weak values if per-key.
  • Two nodes? → In-JVM locks don't help; need DB row locks or a distributed lock with ordering.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a settlement job locked two entities by hashCode order. The deadlock appeared only when a customer migration introduced ids generated from a pattern with collisions. Replacing it with ordering by primary key fixed it permanently.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot find the cycle; blames DB or GC.
  • Hire: Finds hashCode tie, orders by unique key, uses jstack with banner.
  • Strong hire: Also covers computeIfAbsent/map growth, striping, DB-level ordering, and a regression test using colliding strings.

questions.promptHtml: What is thread-pool starvation deadlock? Give an example and the ways to avoid it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common non-lock deadlock in real services; reveals understanding of pools as resources.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A task running on a bounded pool submits subtasks to the same pool and blocks waiting for them. If every worker is occupied by such a parent, the children sit in the queue forever, so no worker ever frees up. The fix is to not block on same-pool children: use separate pools, compose asynchronously (thenCompose), run children in the caller, or use a ForkJoinPool designed for join-with-helping.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
pool(core=max=4, queue)  ->  4 parents run, each does child = pool.submit(..); child.get()
workers: [P1 wait][P2 wait][P3 wait][P4 wait]   queue: [c1][c2][c3][c4]   => stuck

It can happen with pool size 1 and nesting depth 1. Larger pools just raise the load at which it triggers (so it appears under peak traffic). Dump signature: all worker threads WAITING in FutureTask.get/CompletableFuture.join, pool queue length = number of waiting parents, and getActiveCount() == getMaximumPoolSize(). The JVM deadlock detector will NOT flag it. ForkJoinPool mitigates via helping/compensation (join() runs other tasks or adds a compensating thread), but ManagedBlocker is needed for blocking calls.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
// Broken
Future<Integer> parent = pool.submit(() -> pool.submit(() -> compute()).get());
// Fix 1: separate pool for children
ExecutorService childPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
// Fix 2: async composition, no thread blocks
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::step1, pool).thenComposeAsync(r -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> step2(r), childPool), pool);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Increase the pool size": only moves the threshold.
  • CallerRunsPolicy helps only when the pool rejects (needs a bounded/synchronous queue); with an unbounded queue nothing is rejected.
  • Using parallelStream() inside a task running in the common pool and blocking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to bound the damage? → Timeouts on get, bounded queue plus rejection, separate pools per dependency layer.
  2. Why does FJP not deadlock? → join helps execute pending tasks / compensates; but blocking I/O in it still starves.
  3. How do virtual threads change it? → Blocking is cheap so parent-child waiting does not exhaust a small pool, but a semaphore-bounded virtual-thread design can still starve (V1 chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "don't submit-and-wait in the same pool". Senior recognises it from the dump signature, explains why bigger pools only hide it, and designs layer-wise pools or async composition.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fan-out endpoint using one shared @Async executor locked up at the first traffic spike; all 200 workers were parents.

questions.promptHtml: What is priority inversion, and does it matter in Java on Linux?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests OS-level knowledge and honesty about what Java thread priorities actually do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Priority inversion is when a high-priority thread waits on a lock held by a low-priority thread that gets preempted by medium-priority threads, so the high-priority work is effectively delayed by lower-priority work. Famous from Mars Pathfinder, solved with priority inheritance. In Java on typical Linux, thread priorities are not generally honored by default (HotSpot maps them but defaults to ignoring them for normal threads; verify per JDK), so classic inversion is rare, yet the same shape appears at application level: a low-importance job holding a lock or pool slot that critical requests need.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Java: Thread.setPriority(1..10) is a hint; HotSpot on Linux needs privileges/flags (-XX:ThreadPriorityPolicy) to actually change scheduling; by default there is little effect. Avoid relying on it.
  • Intrinsic and ReentrantLock have no priority inheritance.
  • Application-level inversion: background reindexer holds a table-level lock for 30 s, API threads wait. Or a low-priority task occupying all slots of a shared pool.
  • Mitigations: keep critical sections short, never do I/O under a lock, isolate resources (separate pools/locks per priority class), use timeouts, avoid sharing locks between latency-critical and batch paths. In real-time contexts, use RTOS or OS-level priority inheritance (not JVM).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Thread.MAX_PRIORITY to "fix" slowness.
  • Assuming priority inheritance exists in Java locks.
  • Holding the shared lock across a remote call from the low-priority path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fix in a service? → Bulkheads and copy-on-write snapshots so readers never wait for batch writers.
  2. How to detect? → Lock-wait profiling (JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter), per-class latency.
  3. Why not priority queues? → They reorder waiting work; they do not preempt running tasks and can starve low priority (Q183).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the definition. Senior states Java priorities are weak on Linux, and spots the application-level version.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly compaction took a shared lock for 40 s and froze the read path; moving to snapshot reads removed the stall.

questions.contextHtml:
Order API (Spring MVC on Tomcat, 200 max threads, 6 pods, ~1,800 RPS total, normal p99 120 ms). At 14:05 p99 jumps to 30 s then requests time out; the load balancer marks pods unhealthy one by one. CPU 4%, heap 55%, GC pauses < 20 ms. jcmd Thread.print on one pod shows 198 http-nio-8080-exec-* threads:

"http-nio-8080-exec-41" WAITING (parking)
  at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park
  at com.zaxxer.hikari.util.ConcurrentBag.borrow
  at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection

No "Found one Java-level deadlock" banner. Hikari maximumPoolSize=20, connectionTimeout=30000. A new feature that day calls a partner API inside a @Transactional method with a 60 s read timeout.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now, and what is the root cause?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase Tomcat threads and DB pool" or "restart and hope". Ignores that the dump already says every thread waits for a connection and nobody says who holds them.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What deployed at ~14:00? Is the partner API slow (its p99)? Do other pods behave the same? What is hikaricp_connections_active/pending and DB pg_stat_activity state ("idle in transaction")?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back or feature-flag the partner call off; if not possible, set a short client timeout (2 s) and circuit breaker. Restart pods only after capturing dumps.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Connections held across a slow external call inside a transaction (20 connections each tied up for up to 60 s). (b) DB lock wait/long transaction. (c) Connection leak. Red herring: Tomcat thread count; they are victims.
  4. How I'd verify: Dump the 20 threads that hold connections (the ones NOT parked at borrow): they will be in socket read inside the partner HTTP client under @Transactional. Hikari leak detection (leakDetectionThreshold), Prometheus hikaricp_connections_pending, pg_stat_activity showing idle in transaction.
  5. Root cause: Connection held while doing network I/O. Capacity math: 20 connections, each held ~60 s when the partner is slow, gives 20/60 = 0.33 req/s throughput through that path versus 1,800/6 = 300 RPS per pod arriving; the other 180 threads queue for a connection (30 s timeout), all 200 threads blocked. It is starvation of a resource, not a lock cycle, so no banner.
  6. Fix: Short: remove the partner call from the transaction, set tight connect/read timeouts, add a bulkhead (semaphore) for the partner path. Long: transaction scope = DB work only; outbox pattern for external effects.
// Do external I/O outside the transaction
PartnerResult r = partner.call(req);          // timeout 2s, bulkhead
txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(s -> repo.save(r.toEntity()));
  1. Prevention: Alert on pending connections > 0 for 30 s; leakDetectionThreshold; ArchUnit/lint rule banning remote clients in @Transactional; load-test with a slow stub dependency.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise the pool to 100: it moves the bottleneck to the DB and amplifies the next stall. Not lengthen timeouts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the LB take pods out one by one? → Health check needs a thread or a connection; it also timed out, causing cascading load onto survivors.
  • Pool is already sized right, partner is down for an hour? → Circuit breaker returning fast fallback, bulkhead so only that endpoint degrades.
  • Why no deadlock banner? → No cycle: the holders will eventually finish; the JVM detector only sees lock cycles.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "tiny" tax-calculation call added inside a transaction took 90 minutes of incident time to find because everyone stared at DB CPU. The 20 holders were all in one HTTP client frame.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scales Tomcat/pool; no dump reading.
  • Hire: Reads dump, finds holders in network call, moves call outside the transaction.
  • Strong hire: Does the capacity math, adds bulkhead/circuit breaker/health-check separation, and prevention gates.

questions.promptHtml: Throughput plateaus at 8 of 32 cores and CPU is only 25%. How do you prove lock contention is the cause and find which lock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who guess "add threads" from those who measure waiting time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Low CPU with a throughput ceiling and many threads BLOCKED or parked means waiting, not computing. I confirm with repeated thread dumps (counting threads waiting to lock the same address), then identify the lock and its hold time with JFR (jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, jdk.JavaMonitorWait, jdk.ThreadPark) or async-profiler in lock mode (-e lock). Then I shorten the critical section, shard the lock, or remove sharing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Triage: top -H per-thread CPU; jstack/jcmd Thread.print -l x5. Many threads BLOCKED (on object monitor) at one <0x...> is the signature for synchronized; for ReentrantLock, threads are WAITING (parking) and the owner shows in "Locked ownable synchronizers".
  2. Quantify: JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter events have a default threshold (20 ms in the default profile, 10 ms in profile; verify for your JDK) so only long waits are recorded, with the monitor class and stack. jdk.ThreadPark covers j.u.c locks. async-profiler: -e lock (monitor contention) gives flame graph weighted by wait time.
  3. Interpret via Amdahl: if a critical section is 10% of the request time and serialized, max speedup = 1/0.1 = 10x regardless of cores. Lock utilization = arrival rate x hold time; when it approaches 1, queueing explodes.
  4. Remedies, in order of cost: do less under the lock (move I/O, logging, allocation outside), reduce sharing (thread-local/accumulate-then-merge, LongAdder), split (striping, ConcurrentHashMap), use read-mostly structures (copy-on-write, StampedLock optimistic reads), or redesign (single-writer/actor).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=lock settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/lock.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter /tmp/lock.jfr | head -50
# async-profiler (path/version per install)
asprof -e lock -d 30 -f /tmp/lock.html <pid>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding threads: more waiters, more context switches, lower throughput.
  • Sampling only CPU profiles: blocked threads are invisible to a CPU profiler.
  • Treating a busy-but-hot lock as a bug when hold time is fine and the real fix is capacity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a lock held 1 ms with 100 us interarrival a problem? → Utilization 10 (1 ms/0.1 ms) means the queue grows unboundedly; max throughput 1000/s.
  2. Why can fixing one lock reveal another? → The bottleneck moves (Amdahl); re-profile.
  3. How do you detect contention on ConcurrentHashMap.compute? → It locks the bin; hot key shows as synchronized frames inside CHM in the lock profile.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE runs jstack once. Senior uses sampled dumps plus JFR/async lock profiles, computes utilization/Amdahl bounds, and picks the remedy by hold time vs sharing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A global SimpleDateFormat-guarded or logging appender lock capping a 32-core box at 8 cores of useful work is the textbook finding.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout (Service A) calls Inventory (Service B) over HTTP with 3 retries, 5 s timeout, no jitter. A has 8 pods x 200 Tomcat threads and a shared HTTP client pool of 100 connections per pod; B has 4 pods x 100 threads. Normal: 2,000 RPS into A, B p99 40 ms. At 02:10 a B deploy introduces a slow DB query: B p99 rises to 4 s. By 02:14 A p99 is 20 s, A returns 503, B's CPU at 95% and its request count is 3x normal, even though A's inbound RPS is flat. A's dumps: 190+ threads in PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager.leaseConnection/socket read. B rolled back at 02:20 but A and B stay degraded until 02:40.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure mechanism and why recovery lagged the rollback. How do you make this system safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "B was slow, so A was slow; scale both." Misses retry amplification and the fact that queued work continues after the cause is gone.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are retries on timeouts for non-idempotent calls? Is there a circuit breaker/bulkhead? What are A's client pool pending-lease and B's accept queue? Did autoscaling add pods mid-incident?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable retries (flag) and enable load shedding at A for inventory calls; fail fast with cached/stale inventory; rate-limit A to B; scale B only if its DB can take it (it can't, the query is the problem).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Retry amplification: each A request becomes up to 4 calls to B, 2,000 x 4 = 8,000 RPS offered vs B capacity at 4 s latency: 400 threads / 4 s = 100 RPS. (b) A's threads/connections all pinned waiting (Little's law: concurrency = RPS x latency = 2,000 x 20 s = 40,000 needed vs 1,600 threads). (c) Thread-pool starvation of health checks. Red herring: network, GC.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare B inbound RPS vs A outbound count; A's client metrics (pending leases, retry counters); thread dump state counts; B's DB slow-query log.
  5. Root cause: A positive feedback loop. Slow dependency leads to timeouts, which cause retries (extra load), which slow it more (metastable failure). A's threads blocked up to 4 x 5 s = 20 s per request, so its capacity fell to 1,600/20 = 80 RPS. After rollback, B still had a backlog of queued and retried requests; the stale queue and the in-flight retries kept it saturated until the work drained (about 20 min). The system had a stable bad state.
  6. Fix: Short: retries budget (e.g. at most 10% extra), exponential back-off with jitter, per-try timeout under the remaining deadline, circuit breaker, bulkhead (semaphore, max 50 concurrent calls to B) so A keeps serving other endpoints. Long: deadline propagation, load shedding at B (reject when queue > N, return 429/503), client-side concurrency limits (adaptive), idempotency keys.
// bulkhead: bound the damage a slow dependency can do to this pod
Semaphore inventorySlots = new Semaphore(50);
if (!inventorySlots.tryAcquire(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return fallback();
try { return client.call(req, Duration.ofMillis(800)); } finally { inventorySlots.release(); }
  1. Prevention: Game-day with a slow stub; alerts on retry ratio and pending leases; dashboards of in-flight concurrency per dependency; SLO-based load shedding.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise timeouts or pool sizes (more held resources, slower failure). Not retry on every error. Fail-fast fallback means possibly overselling; accept it with reconciliation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retries are mandated by the client SDK, what do you do? → Wrap with a budget/circuit breaker or disable at the SDK level; retry only at one layer.
  • Why use a semaphore instead of a thread pool for the bulkhead? → No queueing latency, simple, works with virtual threads too.
  • How do you tell recovery lag from a second bug? → Offered load vs completed; if offered drops but B stays saturated, it's backlog.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a recommendation outage lasted 25 min past the rollback because three layers each retried 3 times (3^3 = 27x multiplier). Adding a retry budget at only the edge ended recurrence.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests scaling; no explanation of cascade.
  • Hire: Identifies retry amplification and pool pinning, proposes circuit breaker and timeouts.
  • Strong hire: Does Little's-law math, explains metastable recovery lag, proposes retry budgets, deadline propagation, shedding and bulkheads.

questions.promptHtml: The JVM printed no "Found one Java-level deadlock" but the app is clearly deadlocked. Give me the kinds of deadlock the built-in detector cannot see.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors know the detector's blind spots and can still diagnose.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The detector only finds cycles of threads blocked on object monitors and AbstractOwnableSynchronizer-based locks (e.g. ReentrantLock). It misses waits on things that are not "owned" by a thread: latches, semaphores, Future.get/join, conditions never signalled, a bounded pool starved by its own tasks, DB row locks, distributed locks, and class-initialization cycles in some cases. For those I read what each parked thread waits for and find who should have released or signalled.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hang type Why not detected Dump signature
Pool starvation (Q185) Pool slot has no owner All workers WAITING in Future.get
CountDownLatch never counted down No owner for latch Threads parked at CountDownLatch.await
Semaphore leak (acquire without release in exception path) Semaphore permits unowned Parked in Semaphore.acquire
Lost notify / wait without loop No cycle Threads in Object.wait
Read-to-write upgrade on ReentrantReadWriteLock Detector reportedly misses it (OpenJDK bug reports mention gaps; verify) Thread parked in WriteLock.lock while holding read lock
DB deadlock/lock wait Outside JVM Threads in socket read to DB
Class init cycle (Q193) Class init lock not an ordinary monitor Frames in <clinit>

Approach: classify every non-idle thread by what it waits on, then ask "who must act for this to proceed, and is that thread itself waiting?". Draw the wait-for graph by hand. Complement with timeouts everywhere (await(timeout), get(timeout), tryLock), and a watchdog metric on pool queue age.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Leak: permit lost when task throws
sem.acquire();
doWork();            // throws -> release never called
sem.release();
// Fix
sem.acquire();
try { doWork(); } finally { sem.release(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Concluding "not a deadlock" when the banner is absent.
  • Fixing symptoms by restart; no timeouts to bound the next occurrence.
  • Condition.await() without predicate loop and with signal before await.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't the JVM detect latch deadlocks? → No thread "owns" the latch; any thread could count down.
  2. What do you add to make them detectable? → Timeouts that log the wait-for state; metrics for queue age and in-flight count.
  3. Can a deadlock span processes? → Yes (DB, distributed locks); detect with lock-wait timeouts and DB views.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE trusts the banner. Senior knows what it covers, builds the wait-for graph manually, and bakes in timeouts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leaked semaphore permit on an exception path slowly strangled an endpoint over days; no dump ever showed a banner.

questions.promptHtml: Why can a connection pool deadlock itself, and what pool size guarantees it can't (HikariCP's guidance)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of resource deadlock where a thread holds one connection and asks for another.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If a thread holds a connection and requests a second one (nested transaction REQUIRES_NEW, or a helper that opens its own connection), then under load all pool connections can be held by threads each waiting for another. Nobody can finish, nobody releases. Hikari's guidance for the guaranteed-safe minimum is pool size = Tn x (Cm - 1) + 1, where Tn is max concurrent threads and Cm is max connections one thread holds simultaneously.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Example from Hikari's pool-sizing notes: 3 threads each needing 4 connections gives 3 x (4 - 1) + 1 = 10. Reasoning: if the pool holds that many, at least one thread can always get its full set, finish, and release. With Tn = 200 Tomcat threads and Cm = 2 (e.g. REQUIRES_NEW), you'd need 200 x 1 + 1 = 201 connections: infeasible, so the right fix is to not nest: restructure to use one connection per thread, or limit concurrency on the nested path with a semaphore sized below the pool. The wait ends only by connectionTimeout expiring (default 30 s in HikariCP; verify), failing requests instead of hanging forever.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Transactional
public void outer() {
    repo.save(a);
    inner.audit();           // @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW): 2nd connection
}                            // outer holds #1 while waiting for #2 -> pool self-deadlock under load

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enlarging the pool to "fix" it: just raises the load threshold.
  • Test with 1-2 threads; the bug appears only when concurrency >= pool size.
  • Forgetting libraries that grab their own connection (job scheduler, audit, ID generator).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternative to REQUIRES_NEW? → Record audit in the same transaction, or after commit via outbox/event.
  2. How to bound it cheaply? → Semaphore of poolSize/2 around the nested section; timeouts.
  3. Symptom? → hikaricp_connections_pending high, active = max, DB shows many "idle in transaction".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "pool exhausted". Senior knows the formula, why it's usually impractical, and removes the nesting.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A REQUIRES_NEW audit write froze a service at pool size 20 once concurrency hit 20; every request waited 30 s then failed.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing cache refresh serves ~5,000 RPS. After adding "refresh if stale" the service stalls permanently within minutes of deploy; CPU 1%. One thread dump line stands out in every worker:

"http-exec-17" WAITING (parking)
  at ...ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock
  at PriceCache.get(PriceCache.java:31)

Code:

private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
Price get(String sku) {
    rw.readLock().lock();
    try {
        Price p = map.get(sku);
        if (p == null || p.isStale()) {
            rw.writeLock().lock();          // upgrade
            try { p = load(sku); map.put(sku, p); }
            finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
        }
        return p;
    } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
}
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, why does it hang, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Writer starvation, make the lock fair." Fairness doesn't change it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it every thread or only on stale entries? Is load a remote call? Any other lock holders?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back; or temporarily disable stale refresh.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Read-to-write upgrade: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not support upgrading. A thread holding the read lock requesting the write lock blocks until all read locks (including its own) are released: self-deadlock. (b) Two readers both attempt upgrade: each waits for the other's read lock. Red herring: GC, DB.
  4. Verify: Dump shows the thread parked in WriteLock.lock while Locked ownable synchronizers or the code shows it holds the read lock; reproducible with a single thread and a stale entry.
  5. Root cause: Javadoc states upgrade from read to write is not possible. Even a single thread deadlocks on itself, since write acquisition requires zero readers. Only downgrade (write -> read) is supported.
  6. Fix: Release read lock, take write lock, re-check, load, optionally downgrade.
Price get(String sku) {
    rw.readLock().lock();
    try { Price p = map.get(sku); if (p != null && !p.isStale()) return p; }
    finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
    rw.writeLock().lock();
    try {
        Price p = map.get(sku);                       // re-check: another thread may have loaded
        if (p == null || p.isStale()) { p = load(sku); map.put(sku, p); }
        return p;
    } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
}

Better: no remote load under a global write lock; use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent-style per-key loading or Caffeine LoadingCache (single-flight per key). 7. Prevention: Unit test with a stale entry on one thread; lint on nested read/write lock calls. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not StampedLock.tryConvertToWriteLock as a quick patch (not reentrant, more complex). Not hold the write lock across the remote load: it blocks all reads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the write-lock holding load a problem? → Every reader blocks for the duration of a remote call.
  • Does the deadlock detector flag it? → Possibly not; don't rely on it.
  • Why re-check after taking the write lock? → Between unlock and relock another thread may have refreshed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a config reloader deadlocked itself on a single thread in staging, because staging had no stale entries path until a flag flipped in prod.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests fair lock or larger pool.
  • Hire: Names no-upgrade rule, fixes with release/re-check.
  • Strong hire: Moves loading out of the lock with single-flight per key, adds test, discusses StampedLock trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: Can class initialization cause a deadlock? Explain how and how you'd spot it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A subtle, real hazard that shows deep JVM understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Yes. The JVM guarantees a class is initialized once, by taking an initialization lock; if class A's static initializer touches class B while another thread initializes B whose static initializer touches A, each thread holds one init lock and waits for the other. Typical triggers are static singletons referencing each other, or static init spawning threads that use the class being initialized.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: JLS 12.4.2 describes the procedure with per-class initialization locks, with the thread-current-initialization check for recursion. Two threads initializing in opposite order yields a cycle. Thread dumps show frames in <clinit> and threads RUNNABLE or in Class.forName0/ensureClassInitialized, and the standard deadlock detector may not report it (OpenJDK bug reports on intertwined <clinit> exist; verify for your version). Another variant: static { executor.submit(() -> Foo.x).get(); }: the worker needs Foo initialized, which the initializing thread is blocked on.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class A { static final B B_INST = new B(); static int x = 1; }
class B { static final int y = A.x; }   // T1: A.<clinit> needs B; T2: B.<clinit> needs A

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Starting threads or doing I/O in static initializers.
  • Circular static dependencies between singletons.
  • Thinking final constants always trigger init (compile-time constants are inlined and don't).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to avoid it? → No cross-class static cycles; lazy holder idiom; dependency injection; keep <clinit> trivial.
  2. Why does it occur only at startup under load? → Needs two threads racing to first use in opposite order.
  3. How to diagnose? → Thread dump with <clinit> frames in several threads; look at which class each is initializing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE has never heard of it. Senior can explain the init lock model and recognise <clinit> frames.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: App sometimes hung at startup in prod (parallel warmup) but never in dev (sequential); the culprit was two enum/static registries referencing each other.

questions.contextHtml: A rate limiter / metrics service keeps Map<String, Stats> stats = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()), with Stats fields updated under synchronized(this). At 5,000 RPS across 3 pods (16 cores each) CPU is 20% and p99 is 15 ms. Product expects 10x traffic (50,000 RPS) via Black Friday. A load test at 20,000 RPS shows throughput flat at ~17,000, CPU 35%, p99 380 ms; JFR shows jdk.JavaMonitorEnter dominated by the synchronized map; 1,500 distinct keys but 40% of traffic hits 5 hot keys.
questions.promptHtml: How do you redesign it to hold 50,000 RPS without moving to a new datastore?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ConcurrentHashMap" and stop: still contends on hot-key Stats locks, and compute still serializes per bin/key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do reads need exact real-time values or is ~1 s staleness OK? Is the stats object counters only? Are reads rare vs writes? Must data survive restart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce per-request work under lock (move logging/serialization out) and shed non-critical stat updates under pressure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Global map lock serializes every request: utilization = 17,000 x hold time (~58 us each) approaches 1. (b) Hot keys contend on per-object locks. (c) False sharing on counters. Red herring: GC (no pauses > 10 ms).
  4. How I'd verify: async-profiler -e lock; JFR monitor events by class; microbenchmark with JMH (threads = 16) comparing variants.
  5. Root cause: Amdahl: a single serialized section. If hold time is 55 us, max throughput = 1/55 us = ~18,000/s, matching the plateau.
  6. Fix: ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> (or a small stats object with LongAdder fields) so map lookup is lock-free for reads and hot-key increments are striped across cells; pre-register keys with computeIfAbsent once. Reads (sum()) are not atomic snapshots: acceptable for metrics. If a consistent multi-field snapshot is needed, use per-thread/per-shard accumulation merged periodically, or a single-writer thread draining a queue.
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void record(String key) { hits.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); }
// computeIfAbsent on an existing key in Java 8 locks the bin; fast-path get first:
LongAdder a = hits.get(key); if (a == null) a = hits.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()); a.increment();
  1. Prevention: JMH benchmark in CI with thread scaling; load tests at 2x target; ban synchronizedMap for hot paths in review.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: LongAdder.sum() may miss concurrent updates (weakly consistent) and uses more memory per counter. I would not use AtomicLong for the hot keys (CAS retries under contention) and not shard by thread id without a merge strategy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 100% accurate snapshots needed? → Periodic swap of buffers (double-buffering) or a lock only for snapshot, not for increments.
  • Why not ReadWriteLock? → Increments are writes; no read concurrency to exploit.
  • Cache-line effects? → LongAdder pads cells (@Contended), avoiding false sharing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: replacing a synchronized counter map with LongAdder raised the ceiling 6x and moved the bottleneck to JSON serialization; plan for the next bottleneck.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only says ConcurrentHashMap or more pods.
  • Hire: Identifies serialized section, uses CHM + LongAdder, mentions weak consistency.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies via hold time/Amdahl, benchmarks with JMH, addresses hot keys, snapshot semantics and next bottleneck.

questions.promptHtml: Two requests hit "Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction" in the database. How is this different from a JVM deadlock, and how do you handle it in application code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Backend engineers must handle deadlocks that no JVM tool will show.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The DB detects a cycle of row/table locks between transactions and kills one as the victim, so the application sees an exception it must handle. Prevention is the same idea as in the JVM: consistent ordering of updates (by primary key), short transactions, and appropriate indexes (so fewer rows are locked). Handling: retry the whole transaction a bounded number of times with jitter, only if it is safe (idempotent).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Typical cause: T1 updates row 1 then row 2; T2 updates row 2 then row 1. Others: gap/next-key locks (MySQL InnoDB, repeatable read), missing indexes causing wide scans, foreign key checks, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in different order. Different DBs: PostgreSQL raises 40P01 deadlock_detected after deadlock_timeout (default 1 s; verify) and aborts one; InnoDB detects immediately and rolls back the one with fewer changes (verify). Retry must restart the whole unit of work, not just the failing statement, and must not re-run external side effects.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try { return tx.execute(s -> transfer(a, b, amt)); }
    catch (CannotAcquireLockException | DeadlockLoserDataAccessException e) { // Spring translations
        if (attempt >= 3) throw e;
        Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(10, 50L << attempt));
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying inside the same (now rolled-back) transaction.
  • Retrying non-idempotent side effects (emails, payments).
  • Updating rows in arbitrary order in batch jobs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to reduce frequency? → Sort keys before updating, keep transactions short, add indexes, lower isolation level where valid.
  2. Can JVM lock + DB lock mix deadlock? → Yes: thread holds a monitor and waits for a DB lock held by a transaction waiting for that monitor; no detector sees it. Avoid holding JVM locks across DB calls.
  3. How to observe? → DB deadlock logs (SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, Postgres log), app metric on retries.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE retries blindly. Senior orders updates, shortens transactions, retries idempotently with jitter, and warns about cross-system cycles.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly batch updating the same rows as the API in different order produced a few deadlock errors per hour until it sorted by id.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review of a 47-minute full outage of a payment-orchestration service (6 pods, 200 worker threads each, shared @Async executor core=max=32, queue=10,000). Timeline: 11:02 traffic +30%; 11:05 p99 from 90 ms to 12 s; 11:09 pods fail liveness probes (they run on the same executor); 11:11 Kubernetes restarts pods in a loop; 11:49 recovered after manual scale-down of upstream. Dumps taken at 11:07 show 32 executor threads WAITING in CompletableFuture.join, queue length 9,870. No deadlock banner. The @Async method fans out to 3 sub-calls, each also @Async on the same executor, then joins.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: root cause, contributing factors, and the action items you'd prioritize.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Executor too small, raise to 200, add alerts." Treats a design deadlock as a capacity problem and ignores the liveness-probe and restart-loop amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why did the probes use the busy executor? Did restarts drop in-flight payments? What changed at 11:02 (traffic only)? Are the sub-calls idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what was done / should have been): Restore service by killing the queue, restarting with traffic gated (readiness off), then ramp up; rollback or disable the fan-out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pool-starvation deadlock: parents occupy all 32 threads waiting for children queued behind them. (b) Liveness probe sharing the executor killed healthy-ish pods, resetting caches and causing thundering herd. (c) Unbounded-ish queue (10,000) hid backpressure and added minutes of latency to every task.
  4. How to verify: Dump: 32 workers in join, children in the queue; check ratio queue length vs workers; thread names; probe handler thread name; Kubernetes events for restart cadence.
  5. Root cause: Nested @Async fan-out on the same fixed pool: with 32 threads, once 32 parents run concurrently (32 / 4 tasks per parent ratio breaks at modest load), children never get a thread. Traffic +30% crossed the threshold; below it, spare threads let children run. Not a lock cycle, so no banner.
  6. Fix: Short: separate executor for children (or run children inline), get/join with timeouts, bounded queue with CallerRunsPolicy or reject with 503, probes on a dedicated thread/endpoint, readiness vs liveness split. Long: async composition (thenCombine) without blocking joins; per-dependency bulkheads; load shedding.
// no thread blocks: parent returns a future; children use their own pool
CompletableFuture<A> a = supplyAsync(this::callA, childPool);
CompletableFuture<B> b = supplyAsync(this::callB, childPool);
return a.thenCombine(b, Result::new).orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // Java 9+
  1. Prevention (action items, ranked): (1) Remove blocking join on same pool; (2) liveness independent of app executors; (3) bounded queue, size = target latency x throughput (e.g. 1 s x 500/s = 500, not 10,000); (4) metrics: queue age, active/max, rejected count; (5) load test at 2x with synthetic dependency latency; (6) blameless review checklist: "does any task wait on another task of the same pool?".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not only enlarge the pool (hides, then recurs at higher load). Not turn off liveness probes entirely. Reject policies shed some payments; acceptable if clients retry idempotently and it beats total outage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did restarts make it worse? → Cold JIT and caches plus synchronized retry bursts (thundering herd) slowed recovery.
  • Where would virtual threads help? → Blocking join is cheap per virtual thread, but the shared bounded executor design (if kept) still needs removal; verify pinning (V1 chunk).
  • How do you present blame-free? → Describe the system conditions that made the mistake easy (shared default executor, no queue-age alert).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after a similar review, the team added one automated check: an integration test that runs the endpoint with pool size 1 and a 2-level fan-out; it would have hung and caught the bug in CI.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Capacity-only answer; no root-cause mechanism.
  • Hire: Identifies nested same-pool dependency, fixes with separate pool or async composition, separates probes.
  • Strong hire: Adds quantified queue sizing, restart-loop analysis, CI test with pool size 1, ranked action items with owners and metrics.
